# IronGall v1 test vectors

Files any IronGall implementation can check itself against, made with stock tools only (`generate.sh`: bash, od, base64, sha256sum, ssh-keygen, and age ≥ 1.3 for the one ciphertext). Every vector is judged at the time in `now`.

**The keys are public test keys.** The Ed25519 ones are RFC 8032's (`input/*.ed25519`: the seed, then the public key, in hex): from §7.1, box A's identity is TEST 1 and box B's is TEST 2, A's working key is TEST 3, B's is TEST 1024, and a second working key of A's is TEST SHA(abc); from §7.2, box C's working key is the first Ed25519ctx test's key. Box C's identity is of the optional type `ecdsa-sha2-nistp256`: the test key of RFC 6979 §A.2.5 (`input/c.p256`: the private scalar, then the public point as x and y, in hex). The age recipients in `input/` are public keys whose secret keys were discarded, so nothing here decrypts.

| Path | What | Expected |
|---|---|---|
| `a/`, `b/` | each box's `identity.doc` and `address`; `work-cert.pub`, its identity's certificate for its working key; its prekey statements `prekey-<serial>.txt` with `.sig`, signed by the working key; A's `revoke.txt` with `revoke.sig`, its revocation, signed by the identity itself, and `revoke.sha256.sig`, the same with SHA-256, which verifiers accept; and A's `pass.txt`, `pass.sig` and `pass.authorization`, a pass for a server it calls `irongall.example` | all valid. `a/prekey-1` is post-quantum, `a/prekey-2` X25519 only (`--no-pq`); `a/prekey-1.txt.sha256.sig` signs with SHA-256 instead of SHA-512, which verifiers accept. The pass runs out ten minutes after `now` |
| `c/` | box C, whose identity is a P-256 key: its `identity.doc` (173 bytes) and `address`, `work-cert.pub`, `prekey-1.txt` with `.sig`, and `revoke.txt` with `revoke.sig`, its revocation, made once and kept | valid for a client that verifies `ecdsa-sha2-nistp256`. One that does not refuses the document with its code for a key type it lacks, never as malformed |
| `cert/bad-*` | a certificate (`.pub`) that breaks one rule, and a signature made under it (`.sig`) over `a/prekey-1.txt` in A's prekey namespace | every one refused for box A. The signature is good under the certificate it carries: the certificate is what fails. `bad-serial-above-2-53` is numbered 2^53, one above the highest serial. `ssh-keygen -Y verify` alone takes `bad-extensions`, `bad-key-id` and `bad-serial-zero` |
| `revoke/bad-*.sig` | a signature that is not a revocation of box A: `bad-by-a-working-key` (A's working key over A's statement, under A's own certificate), `bad-by-another-identity` (B's identity over A's statement), `bad-another-namespace` (A's identity over A's statement, in the prekey namespace), `bad-of-another-box` (A's identity over B's statement), `bad-s-plus-l` (A's own revocation, with L added to its S) | every one refused as a revocation of A. `ssh-keygen -Y verify` takes `bad-by-a-working-key` when the identity is named a `cert-authority`, so a verifier's signers line for a revocation never says so |
| `revoked/ok-*` | a list of box A's revoked certificates (`.txt`) and A's identity's signature over it (`.sig`): `ok-one-range` (version 1, serials 1 to 4, with `.sha256.sig` in the other hash) and `ok-serials-and-ranges` (version 7: 2, 5 to 9, 11, and the highest serial there is) | taken as lists of A's revoked certificates, each naming exactly those serials |
| `revoked/bad-*` | what is not a list of A's revoked certificates, each with a signature that is good over its bytes: `bad-by-a-working-key` (A's working key, under A's own certificate), `bad-another-namespace` (A's identity, in the revocation's namespace), `bad-another-address` (B's address in it), and one for each rule of the text (no serial, a version or a serial of zero, with a leading zero, of 19 digits or above 2^53 − 1, a range backwards or of one, serials descending or overlapping, a blank line, a trailing space, CRLF, no final newline, another tag, the address in uppercase, a NUL); and `bad-s-plus-l`, a good list whose signature has L added to its S | every one refused. `ssh-keygen -Y verify` takes each of the malformed ones, since the signature is good: the text is what fails, and a shell reader that tests a variable alone takes `bad-nul`. It takes `bad-s-plus-l` too, on an OpenSSH built on its own Ed25519, as it takes `revoke/bad-s-plus-l` |
| `sig/ok-*`, `sig/bad-*` | `a/prekey-1.txt.sig` in other forms, each over `a/prekey-1.txt` in A's prekey namespace, under A's certificate (PROTOCOL.md §3). `ok-*`: CRLF line ends, CRLF after the BEGIN line only, a space and a tab in the base64, a VT and an FF there, a blank line before the END line, the base64 on one line, no line feed after the END line, text after it, the file padded after it to exactly 4096 bytes, and a blob whose `reserved` field holds bytes the key did not sign. `bad-*`: 4097 bytes, after the END line or as spaces before it; a space after the BEGIN line, text before it, no END line, an END line indented; a character outside base64, a NUL, a padding bit set, the padding gone; a byte after the blob's five fields; and an Ed25519 S with L added, the working key's (`bad-s-plus-l`) or the identity's on the certificate (`bad-certificate-s-plus-l`) | `ok-*` taken, `bad-*` refused, as `ssh-keygen -Y verify` judges each but four: it takes both of 4097 bytes, and on an OpenSSH built on its own Ed25519 (10.2p1, Ubuntu) both S + L. Those a verifier refuses by its own checks |
| `cert/ok-*` | a certificate at the edge of a rule, and a signature made under it, as `cert/bad-*` | taken. `ok-begins-now` begins at `now`; `bad-not-begun` begins a second later |
| `message/` | `a-to-b.line`, an envelope from A to B as its one line; `a-to-b.sig`, A's working key's signature over it for B; `a-to-b.plain`, what is encrypted (the line, the signature, the padding); `a-to-b.age`, that encrypted to B's prekey | the line and the signature are what a client makes from the same keys, byte for byte; the age file is a whole number of blocks |
| `plain/accept-*`, `refuse-*` | what box B decrypts | delivered or refused, as named, with these codes: `refuse-no-line-feed`, `-no-signature`, `-blank-line-before-the-signature`, `-signature-first`, `-no-end-line`, `-end-line-without-its-line-feed`, `-crlf` and `-envelope-on-two-lines` as `bad_message`; `refuse-signature-over-4096-bytes` (spaces in its base64) as `bad_signature`; `refuse-no-identity`, `-identity-not-base64` and `-identity-of-small-order` as `bad_identity`; `refuse-signed-for-another-box`, `-signed-by-the-identity`, `-signed-by-a-bare-working-key`, `-certificate-ended`, `-line-changed-after-signing` and `-another-box-s-identity-document` as `bad_signature`; `refuse-from-is-not-the-identity`, `-from-is-not-the-identity-of-an-unknown-type` and `-to-another-box` as `reattributed`; `refuse-unsupported-key-type` as `unsupported_key_type`. `accept-p256-sender` is from box C: delivered by a client that verifies `ecdsa-sha2-nistp256`, and `unsupported_key_type` to one that does not. `accept-whitespace-in-the-signature` has a space, a CR and a tab in its base64, which every verifier skips. In `accept-anything-after-the-signature` a second envelope, signed by B, follows the first END line and is never read. `refuse-another-box-s-identity-document` is the forgery an identity member invites: A's document beside a certificate B's identity signed |
| `identity/*.doc` | malformed identity documents, and well-formed ones holding a key that fails its type's checks: a small-order or non-canonical Ed25519 key, or (`p256-*`) a P-256 point that is off the curve, not reduced, or one OpenSSH refuses (`p256-short-coordinate`, `p256-coordinate-over-order`: both are on the curve, and a library may take them). `unsupported-type.doc` is a well-formed document of a key type nobody verifies. `nul-*` and `p256-nul-*` hold a NUL byte, in place of a line feed or elsewhere, and are as long as a good document | every one rejected: `unsupported-type.doc` as a key type the client does not verify, the rest as a bad document or a bad key |
| `prekey/bad-*` | prekey statements with a `.sig` by A's working key, in A's namespace, except where the name says otherwise | every one rejected, `bad-serial-above-2-53` among them: a serial is at most 2^53 − 1, since a send carries it as a JSON number. `bad-outlives-its-certificate` is signed under the certificate beside it, which ends in ten days |
| `prekey/expired` | a valid statement whose `not_after` is `now` | valid, but expired: a sender must not encrypt to it |
| `prekey/longest` | a valid statement that ends 33 days and an hour after `now` | not expired, and the longest a server takes: an hour past what a client asks for |
| `prekey/too-long` | a valid statement that ends a second later than that | not expired, but a server must refuse to publish it |
| `envelope/accept-*`, `refuse-*` | envelopes of a message whose signature by A verified, received by B | accepted or refused, as named. Keys match exactly and none may appear twice, so every reader takes the same values: in `accept-case-variant-key` the body is `"benign"` (`BODY` is an unknown key, ignored); `refuse-duplicate-key` has two `from`s; `refuse-version-string` has `"v":"1"`, which is not the number 1; `refuse-not-utf8` and `refuse-two-objects` are not one UTF-8 JSON object. Strict on what a loose reader lets through: `refuse-msg-id-newline` ends its `msg_id` with a newline, `refuse-subject-number` has a number where a string goes, and `refuse-sent-at-second-60` names a second some date parsers carry into the next minute. The envelope is a JSON text as PROTOCOL.md §0b reads one, its body included: `accept-body-nested-to-32` is taken, and `refuse-body-nested-to-33`, `-key-twice-in-the-body`, `-nan-in-the-body`, `-leading-zero-in-the-body`, `-noncharacter-in-the-body`, `-above-u10ffff-in-the-body` and `-byte-order-mark` are refused. The window of `sent_at` has a vector on each side of each end: `accept-33-days-old` and `refuse-33-days-and-1s-old` (refused as `stale`), `accept-1-hour-ahead` and `refuse-1-hour-and-1s-ahead` (refused as `future`) |
| `json/ok-*`, `json/bad-*` | JSON texts, each breaking one rule of PROTOCOL.md §0b or none: a byte-order mark; bytes that are not UTF-8, an overlong form, a surrogate, a code point above U+10FFFF, a five-byte form; a lone surrogate escaped; a noncharacter written, escaped, in plane 16 and in a name; a control character; a name twice, in a nested object and through an escape; a second value, a bracket or a brace after the object; an array, a string, nothing; `NaN`, `nan`, `-Infinity`, `01`, `+1`, `.5`, `1.`; a trailing comma, single quotes, a vertical tab; and nesting to 33. `ok-*` hold what is allowed: whitespace, any JSON number, every escape, a surrogate pair, the code points beside the noncharacters, one name in two objects, and nesting to 32 | `ok-*` taken and `bad-*` refused, by every reader, whatever kind of text it expects |
| `answer/<kind>-ok-*`, `answer/<kind>-bad-*` | whole answers of a server, of each kind a client reads: `identity`, `list`, `message`, `record` (a revocation record), `receipt` and `problem` (an error). The bad ones: a byte member that is a number, unpadded, wrapped or with its unused bits set; a member twice, null after a value, `NaN` beside the record, a second value, nothing, an array; an integer member that is negative, above 2^53 − 1, a fraction or written with one; a string or an object where another type goes. The ok ones: null members, unknown members, names in another case (which are unknown members: such a record shows nothing), and `{}` | `<kind>-ok-*` taken and `<kind>-bad-*` no answer, as each client reads that kind: a `2xx` revocations answer that is no record stops a drain with the mail still on the server |

Ed25519 signatures are deterministic, so an implementation that signs these statements with these keys, under these certificates, must produce byte-identical `.sig` files. A certificate is made once and kept, since `ssh-keygen` puts a random nonce in one, and so is `message/a-to-b.age`, since age encryption is randomised; everything else regenerates byte for byte.
